newsitem.title: USA: Brown & Williamson to appeal Fla. documents ruling.
newsitem.headline: Brown & Williamson to appeal Fla. documents ruling.

text.p: Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. will appeal a Florida judge's ruling allowing plaintiffs in the Broin secondhand-smoke lawsuit to use 16 confidential documents taken from a law firm working for the company, an lawyer for the company said Friday.
The Brown & Williamson attorney, Edward Moss, said during a pretrial hearing that the company would appeal the ruling to the 3rd Florida District Court of Appeal.
Brown & Williamson Tobacco is a unit of B.A.T Industries Plc.

The scheduled June 2 start of the trial -- in a case filed on behalf of 60,000 flight attendants who claim they were sickened by secondhand tobacco smoke -- will not be affected by the filing of the appeal.
Dade County Circuit Judge Robert Kaye said jury selection would go ahead in spite of the appeal and told attorneys not to use the documents pending the outcome of the appeal.

Kaye also was not expected to rule before Monday on a tobacco industry motion to undo the class-action status of the case or a tobacco industry request that fraud and conspiracy allegations be dropped from the lawsuit.
On Tuesday, Kaye ruled to allow plaintiff lawyers Stanley and Susan Rosenblatt to use 16 of the documents and said 12 others could not be used during the trial.

Brown & Williamson had argued that almost all the papers, although widely available in books and elsewhere, were covered by attorney-client privilege and should not be used against tobacco companies in court.

Friday's hearing also included discussion of whether attorneys could mention during the trial Brooke Group Ltd.'s Liggett Group tobacco subsidiary's litigation settlement and the so-called "global settlement" talks under way between tobacco companies and state governments.
Kaye said that during jury selection attorneys should ask if potential jurors were aware of any tobacco-related litigation, not discuss such specifics.

Kelly Luther, an attorney for Liggett, said Liggett believes a restraining order issued by a judge in West Virginia this month would prevent Liggett from defending itself in the Broin case, and said the company was awaiting further word on the issue from a federal court hearing in West Virginia Friday.

Stanley Rosenblatt said he did not believe the West Virginia ruling on the impact of the Liggett settlement should affect the Broin case. "I am not bound, and my 60,000 clients are not bound, by a West Virginia judge," he said.
